questions.problem: Find the point of intersection of the parabola ${x}^{2}=5(y-3)$ with the $y$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
When the parabola intersects the $y$-axis, we must have $x=0.$ So, we set $x=0$ and solve the resulting equation for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2} & =5(y-3) \\ (0)^{2} & =5(y-3) \\ 0 & =5y-15 \\ 5y & =15 \\ y & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parabola intersects the $y$-axis at $(0,3).$

questions.problem: Find the point of intersection of the parabola ${y}^{2}+13x-15y-2=0$ with the $x$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
When the parabola intersects the $x$-axis, we must have $y=0.$ So, we set $y=0$ and solve the resulting equation for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(0)^{2}+13x-15(0)-2 & =0 \\ 13x-2 & =0 \\ x & =\frac{2}{13}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parabola intersects the $x$-axis at $(\frac{2}{13},0).$

questions.problem: Find the points of intersection of the parabola ${y}^{2}-16x-6y-91=0$ with the $y$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
When the parabola intersects the $y$-axis, we must have $x=0.$ So, we set $x=0$ and solve the resulting equation for $y:$

$$

questions.problem: Find the points of intersection of the parabola ${x}^{2}=\frac{2}{5}(y+2)$ with the $x$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
When the parabola intersects the $x$-axis, we must have $y=0.$ So, we set $y=0$ and solve the resulting equation for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2} & =\frac{2}{5}(0+2) \\ {x}^{2} & =\frac{4}{5} \\ x & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{4}{5}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the intersection points are
 $(\sqrt{\frac{4}{5}},0)$ and $(-\sqrt{\frac{4}{5}},0).$

**From left to right**, the **exact values** of the $x$-intercepts of the parabola shown above are{{field-1}}
and 
{{field-2}}.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the equation of the parabola. From the diagram, we see that the parabola has a vertex at $(1,2)$ and passes through the point $(3,-2).$

The general standard equation of an up- or down-opening parabola with vertex $(h,k)$ is given by

$$
(x-h)^{2}=4p(y-k).
$$

Substituting $(h,k)=(1,2)$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-1)^{2} & =4p(y-2).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we need to find $p.$ Since the parabola passes through the point $(3,-2),$ we substitute $x=3$ and $y=-2$ into the equation and get

$$
\begin{aligned}(3-1)^{2} & =4p(-2-2) \\ 4 & =4p(-4) \\ p & =-\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the parabola is

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-1)^{2} & =-(y-2).\end{aligned}
$$

When the parabola intersects the $x$-axis, we must have $y=0.$ So, we substitute $y=0$ into the equation of the parabola and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-1)^{2} & =-(0-2) \\ (x-1)^{2} & =2 \\ x-1 & =\pm \sqrt{2} \\ x & =1\pm \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, from left to right, the $x$-intercepts are $1-\sqrt{2}$  and $1+\sqrt{2}.$

canonical_examples.problem: Find the points of intersection of the parabola $(y-2)^2=4(x+1)$ with the $y$-axis.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To find the points of intersection of the parabola with the $y$-axis, we set $x=0$ and solve the resulting equation for $y\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}(y-2)^{2} & =4(x+1) \\ (y-2)^{2} & =4(0+1) \\ (y-2)^{2} & =4 \\ y-2 & =\pm 2 \\ y & =2\pm 2 \\ y & =0,4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parabola intersects the $y$-axis $(0,0)$ and $(0,4).$
